newsitem.title: USA: No medical evidence of Gulf War Syndrome - studies.
newsitem.headline: No medical evidence of Gulf War Syndrome - studies.

text.p: Two studies of medical and death records have found no medical evidence of "Gulf War Syndrome" blamed for the unexplainable disorders that afflicted thousands of veterans of the 1991 war against Iraq.
But one study concluded these veterans were more likely to suffer fatal accidents than those who did not serve in the Gulf, a finding also seen among Vietnam War veterans.
Both studies, in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, were expected to add fuel to the debate over the cause -- and reality -- of what U.S. officials call "Persian Gulf Illness."

"These two reports are not likely to end the debate about the health consequences of the Gulf War," Dr. Edward Campion, a Journal deputy editor, said. "The studies ended in 1993 so they may seem irrelevant to veterans who feel sick now."
Those who believe they suffer from the syndrome complain of various problems including fatigue, sleep disorders, headaches and pain in the joints and muscles.

The theory that they were feeling the long-term effects of exposure to Iraqi nerve gas got some circumstantial support from recent Pentagon revelations that some troops may have been in the vicinity when gas was released. But U.S. officials insisted the exposure was too small to cause problems even as they offered compensation to Gulf War veterans who think their disabling symptoms were linked to the conflict.
Comparing the health records of those men and women with soldiers not involved in the conflict, researchers in the two studies attempted to find an unrecognized medical problem.
In the first, Han Kang and Tim Bullman of the Department of Veterans Affairs compared the death rates of 695,516 Gulf War veterans to 746,291 other veterans.

They found a higher death rate among Gulf War soldiers but the increase became insignificant when deaths caused by accidents were removed. Disease did not appear to be a factor; nor did suicide or homicide.

"If there are excess illnesses due to ... Gulf service, they do not appear to have been life-threatening," the pair concluded. They failed also find a cause for the higher accident rates among Gulf War veterans.
They also found that female veterans had higher death rates than males. Again, the reason was unclear.

But the death rates for both males and females were dramatically lower than for the general population -- a finding that was unsurprising because those accepted into the military tend to be healthier.

The second study, led by Dr. Gregory Gray of the Naval Health Research Centre in San Diego, took a similar approach but used hospital records instead of death statistics. They found some differences but said they were inconsistent.

For example Gulf War veterans tended to have more cancer-type growths -- but only in 1991, not in 1992 or 1993. Genital and urinary tract problems were higher only in 1991. Diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs were more common in 1992 and mental disorders in 1992 and 1993.

Gray and his colleagues noted that it is common for drug and alcohol use to go up after combat and argued that some of the increases were probably artificial, caused when the veterans finally received treatment for pre-existing medical problems such as benign growths and infertility.
"The data suggest that veterans of the Gulf War who remained on active duty were not at increased risk for unexplained hospitalization during the 25 months after the war," they said.

"Given the wide publicity, the strong beliefs and the political implications, it may be impossible for science ever to establish whether serving in the ... Gulf War really caused a disease that produces only a wide range of symptoms," Campion said.

He advised doctors to "resist the pressure to diagnose a disease for which scientific evidence is lacking" even while acknowledging to the veterans that medical knowledge is imperfect and offering respect "for the veterans who faced the risks of war in the ... Gulf."
